canary: If this tiny bird fell over...
Down here, the deadliest danger was invisible.
A man could breathe it... and never notice.
Scientist John Haldane had found this gas behind deadly mine explosions.
His idea? Send a small bird down first.
Its tiny body breathes so fast, the gas hits it first.
So the men kept glancing at it... all day long.
But here's the part almost nobody knows.
Some cages had their own OXYGEN tank.
Rescue teams carried them into poisoned tunnels.
Shut the little door, open the valve...
and the bird could be REVIVED.
British mines kept canaries until nineteen eighty-six.
A tiny bird... watching over every man underground.
detonator: They used to put EXPLOSIVES on train tracks...
This little metal disc is a railway detonator.
About the size of a coin.
It's strapped to the rail with two soft lead clips.
In thick fog, drivers couldn't see the signals.
Red or green... it all disappeared.
So when a signal showed danger, a fogman placed detonators on the line.
Fogmen stood beside the signals for hours, in the cold.
Usually two or three of them, spaced apart.
A sound no driver could miss... even in total fog.
It meant: DANGER ahead. Slow down... or stop.
Edward Cowper invented it around eighteen forty-one...
and trains still carry detonators today.
A WARNING... loud enough to stop a train.
galveston: This flag warned a whole city that disaster was coming.
Red, with a black square in the middle.
It meant: a STORM is on its way.
Galveston, Texas. September seventh, nineteen hundred.
Weather Bureau chief Isaac Cline watched the waves grow bigger...
and raised the warning flags above the city.
Shops stayed open. People came to the beach to watch the waves.
And Galveston was flat. Its highest point was under nine feet.
The next day, the sky turned black.
Winds over one hundred and thirty miles an hour.
A storm surge over FIFTEEN feet.
The sea swept across the whole island.
At least six thousand people died...
the deadliest natural disaster in American history.
The survivors built a giant seawall... and RAISED their entire city.
That wall still protects Galveston today.
